slides.heading: Collection of Data
slides.body_md: Part 1 — where **data** come from and how an investigator **collects** them.

Designing a questionnaire

visual.caption: Part 1 at a glance

slides.narration: Before any average, graph or conclusion, someone has to collect the facts. Good data make a good study, and careless data spoil it. In this part we learn what primary and secondary data are, three ways of collecting primary data, how to design a questionnaire, and why a small trial run called a pilot survey is worth the effort.

slides.heading: What are data?
slides.body_md: **Data** are the raw material of statistics: facts, figures and observations collected for a purpose.
bullets: Raw data become **information** only after they are organised, presented and analysed.
How good the conclusion is depends on how good the data are.
slides.narration: Data are the raw material of statistics. They are the facts and figures that investigators gather. Raw data on their own say little. Only after they are organised, shown in tables and graphs, and analysed do they turn into information. So the quality of every later step depends on how carefully the data were collected in the first place.

slides.heading: Primary and secondary data
slides.body_md: **Primary data** are collected first-hand by the investigator for a specific purpose. **Secondary data** are collected by someone else and used by the investigator.

rows: The investigator, first-hand, for her own enquiry
Answers from vendors to her own questions on daily sales
Someone else; the investigator only uses them
Sales figures copied from a published dairy board report

visual.alt: Table of definitions: primary data are collected first-hand by the investigator, for example answers from vendors; secondary data are collected by someone else, for example figures copied from a published report
visual.caption: The same table of milk sales can be primary for its collector and secondary for a later user.

slides.narration: Primary data are collected first-hand by the investigator for the enquiry at hand. If you ask Kelvapur milk vendors about their daily sales yourself, those answers are primary data. Secondary data are collected by someone else and only used by you, such as sales figures copied from a published dairy report. The very same table can be primary for its collector and secondary for the next user.

slides.narration: Compare the two on five points. Primary data are original and first-hand, usually costlier and slower to collect, and they fit the enquiry exactly because you design the collection. Secondary data are second-hand, cheaper and quicker, but they may not fit your purpose. So the investigator must check the source and the method before trusting them.

slides.heading: Using secondary data with care
slides.body_md: Published figures were gathered for **someone else's purpose**. Ask four questions before using them.
bullets: **Who** collected the data?
**For what purpose**, and by what **method**?
**When** were they collected?
Do the definitions and units **match** your enquiry?
slides.narration: Secondary data save time and money, but they come with a warning. They were gathered for another purpose, perhaps with different definitions. Before using them, ask who collected them, for what purpose, by what method and when. If the answers do not suit your enquiry, the figures may mislead you, however neat the published table looks.

slides.heading: Quick check: which kind of data?
slides.body_md: A student copies monthly price figures from a dairy board report. Which kind of data are these?
slides.narration: Ask who gathered the figures and for whose purpose. Did the student collect them first-hand, or is she borrowing numbers that someone else collected?

slides.heading: Three methods of collecting primary data

rows: High response; doubts can be cleared
Costly and slow; the interviewer may sway replies
Only people with phones; must be short

visual.alt: Table of three methods of collecting primary data, namely personal interview, which has high response but is costly; mailed questionnaire is cheap with wide coverage but has low response; telephone interview is quick but limited to people with phones and short calls

slides.narration: There are three common ways to collect primary data. In a personal interview the investigator asks questions face to face. In a mailed questionnaire, forms are sent out and returned. In a telephone interview, respondents are questioned by phone. Each has merits and demerits, and the right choice depends on money, time, the number of respondents and how complicated the questions are.

slides.heading: Personal interview
slides.body_md: The investigator meets each respondent and asks the questions in person.
bullets: **Merits:** high response; doubts can be cleared; the interviewer can observe.
**Demerits:** costly and slow over a wide area; the interviewer may **influence** the answers.
Best for a small area and complicated questions.
slides.narration: In a personal interview, the investigator meets the respondent and asks the questions directly. The merits are a high response and the chance to clear doubts on the spot. The demerits are cost and time, especially over a wide area, and the risk that the interviewer influences the answers. It suits small areas and questions that need explaining.

slides.heading: Mailed questionnaire and telephone interview
slides.body_md: Two cheaper ways of reaching respondents.
bullets: **Mailed questionnaire:** low cost and wide coverage, but **low response** and **no clarification** of doubts.
**Telephone interview:** quick, but limited to people who have **telephones**, and the call must be **short**.
slides.narration: A mailed questionnaire is posted or sent by electronic mail. It is cheap and reaches many people, but many forms never come back, and nobody is there to explain a confusing question. A telephone interview is quick, yet it reaches only people who own a phone, and respondents will not stay on a long call.

slides.heading: Quick check: interview strengths and weaknesses
slides.body_md: A personal interview gets a high response and lets doubts be cleared, but it can be costly. True or false?
slides.narration: Think about what the interviewer can do face to face, and about what that costs in travel, staff and time. Then decide whether the statement is true or false.

slides.narration: A questionnaire is a list of questions put to respondents. Follow six steps. Keep it short. Order the questions from general to specific. Make each question precise and clear. Avoid leading questions, double negatives, ambiguous words and questions that embarrass. Mix closed-ended and open-ended questions where suitable. Finally, test it on a few people before the real survey.

slides.heading: Faulty questions and better versions
slides.body_md: Look at four faults from an imagined school canteen survey.

rows: Don't you agree the biryani is wonderful?
How would you rate the biryani? (Poor / Fair / Good)
Is the canteen kept clean? (Yes / No)
How many days a week do you buy snacks?
Do you buy snacks and fruit juice?
Ask about snacks and juice separately

visual.alt: Table of four faulty canteen questions with the fault and a better version: a leading question, a double negative, an ambiguous word and two questions in one

slides.narration: A leading question pushes the respondent towards an answer. A double negative confuses her. An ambiguous word such as often means different things to different people. And a question with two parts, such as snacks and juice, cannot be answered with a single reply. In each case, the better version is neutral, clear and asks just one thing.

slides.heading: Worked example 1: repair a questionnaire
slides.body_md: An imagined canteen survey has the question: Do you not dislike the canteen tea? Repair it step by step.
bullets: Step 1 — Spot the fault: **not** and **dislike** together make a **double negative**.
Step 2 — State what you really want to know: whether the student **likes** the tea.
Step 3 — Rewrite as a **closed-ended** question: Do you like the canteen tea? (Yes / No).
Step 4 — Check: one idea, neutral wording, easy to tabulate.
slides.narration: Take the question: do you not dislike the canteen tea. Step one, spot the fault. The words not and dislike together form a double negative, and a student may answer yes when she means no. Step two, decide what you really want to know: whether she likes the tea. Step three, rewrite it plainly with fixed choices. Step four, check that it asks one thing only.

slides.heading: Closed-ended and open-ended questions
slides.body_md: A questionnaire can use both kinds of question.

rows: Fixed choices: two-way or multiple choice
Do you carry lunch from home? (Yes / No)
What would you change in the canteen menu?

visual.alt: Table comparing closed-ended and open-ended questions with an example of each from an imagined canteen survey

slides.narration: A closed-ended question gives fixed answers to choose from. It may be two-way, with yes or no, or multiple choice. It is easy to tabulate. An open-ended question lets the respondent reply in her own words, which brings out reasons and fresh ideas but is harder to tabulate. A good questionnaire uses each where it suits.

slides.heading: Quick check: type of question
slides.body_md: Do you sell curd along with milk? (Yes / No). What type of question is this?
slides.narration: Look at the answers allowed. If the respondent must pick from fixed choices, the question is closed-ended. If she may reply freely, it is open-ended.

slides.heading: The pilot survey
slides.body_md: A **pilot survey** is a small trial run of the enquiry that tests the questionnaire and gives an estimate of the **cost and time** of the main survey.

nodes.label: Draft the questionnaire
Pilot survey on a few respondents
Find unclear questions; estimate time and cost
Revise and run the main survey

visual.alt: Flow of a pilot survey: draft the questionnaire, try it on a few respondents, find unclear questions and estimate time and cost, then revise and run the main survey
visual.caption: A pilot comes before the main survey

slides.narration: A pilot survey is a small trial run. You try the questionnaire on a few respondents before the real survey. It reveals unclear or badly ordered questions while they are still easy to fix, and it gives a fair estimate of how much time and money the main survey will need. Skipping the pilot can mean discovering faults after thousands of forms are filled.

slides.heading: Worked example 2: choose the method
slides.body_md: Match each imagined situation with a suitable method of collection.
bullets: Step 1 — Note **how many** respondents there are, **where** they live and how **complex** the questions are.
Step 2 — Forty stalls in one lane with a long form: **personal interview**.
Step 3 — Five hundred scattered farmers and a small budget: **mailed questionnaire**.
Step 4 — Sixty office workers with phones and three quick questions: **telephone interview**.

rows: Fieldworkers must visit 40 stalls in one lane and explain a long form
Doubts can be cleared on the spot
Forms must reach 500 farmers across many villages cheaply
Three quick questions to 60 office workers who all have phones

visual.alt: Table choosing a method for three imagined situations: personal interview for 40 stalls in one lane, mailed questionnaire for 500 scattered farmers, telephone interview for 60 office workers with phones

slides.narration: To choose a method, note how many respondents there are, where they live, and how complex the questions are. Forty stalls in one lane with a long form suit personal interviews. Five hundred scattered farmers and a small budget suit a mailed questionnaire. Sixty office workers with phones and three quick questions suit a telephone interview. The situation decides the method.

slides.heading: Quick check: name the trial run
slides.body_md: A trial run of a survey on a few respondents is called a ___ survey.
slides.narration: Recall what an investigator does before the main survey to test the questionnaire on a small group. Use the single word that names this step.

slides.heading: Summary of Part 1

rows: Collected by someone else; check source, purpose, method, date
Short, general to specific, precise, no faults, pilot first

visual.alt: Summary table of Part 1: primary and secondary data, the three methods of collection and the rules for a questionnaire

slides.narration: Let us recap. Data are the raw material of statistics. Primary data are collected first-hand, and secondary data come from someone else and must be checked. The three methods of collecting primary data are personal interview, mailed questionnaire and telephone interview, each with strengths and limits. A good questionnaire is short, ordered, clear and fault-free, and it is tested in a pilot survey first.

slides.heading: Exam tips
bullets: Give the **standard definition** first, then an example.
For compare-type questions, use **a table or numbered points**, one point for each side.
For each method of collection, write **both** a merit and a demerit.
When asked to improve a question, **name the fault**, then rewrite it.
Use your own imagined examples; do not copy examples from the textbook.
slides.narration: Some tips. Begin with the definition, then add an example. In comparison questions, give a point for each side in a table or in numbered points. For each method of collection, always state a merit and a demerit. When asked to improve a question, name the fault first and then rewrite it. And make up your own examples rather than copying from any book.

visual.caption: Census studies every unit; a sample studies a representative part

slides.narration: The population, also called the universe, is the whole group of units about which we want information. The units need not be people. They can be shops, farms or bulbs. A sample is a representative part of that group. Here, the imagined town of Kelvapur has fifty shops. A census studies all fifty. A sample studies only ten, chosen to represent the rest.

slides.heading: The census method
slides.body_md: In the **census method** every unit of the population is studied.
bullets: The result is free of **sampling error**.
It needs much **time, money and staff** when the population is large.
Suitable when the population is **small**, or when detail on **every** unit is needed.
slides.narration: In the census method, every unit of the population is studied. Because nothing is left out, there is no sampling error. The price is paid in time, money and staff, which can be huge for a large population. So a census suits small populations, or enquiries where information on every single unit is essential.

slides.heading: Census versus sample

rows: Population large; units destroyed by testing; limited funds

visual.alt: Table comparing census and sample on coverage, cost, time, accuracy and when each is suitable

slides.narration: Compare them on five points. A census covers every unit, while a sample covers a representative part. A census costs more and takes longer for a large population. A census has no sampling error, but a sample does. A census is suitable for small populations, and a sample for large ones, for limited funds, or when testing destroys the units.

slides.heading: Quick check: what is the population?
slides.body_md: The register of all 50 milk shops of Kelvapur is used for a survey. What are these 50 shops called?
slides.narration: Remember the definition. The complete group of units about which information is wanted has a special name. Decide whether the fifty shops are that complete group, or only a part of it.

slides.heading: Census or sample: how to decide
slides.body_md: Weigh four things before choosing.
bullets: **Size** of the population: small favours a census.
**Cost and time** available.
**Accuracy** needed.
Whether studying a unit **destroys** it.
slides.narration: Four things decide the choice. The first is the size of the population. A small group favours a census. The second is the money and time available. The third is how accurate the result must be. The fourth is whether studying a unit destroys it. If it does, as when bulbs are burned to failure, only a sample can be tested.

slides.heading: Worked example 1: census or sample?
slides.body_md: Choose a method for each imagined case.
bullets: Step 1 — Ask: is the population small, and is every unit needed?
Step 2 — A cooperative of 25 members wants every view: **census**.
Step 3 — A batch of 5,000 fuses tested until they break: **sample**, since testing destroys them.
Step 4 — A quick price check across 800 shops on a small budget: **sample**.

visual.caption: Two families of sampling, five methods

slides.narration: Sampling methods fall into two families. In random sampling every unit has an equal chance of selection. Two methods are the lottery method and random number tables. In non-random sampling, the investigator or interviewer has a hand in the choice. Three methods are judgement sampling, convenience sampling and quota sampling.

slides.heading: Random sampling
slides.body_md: In **random sampling** every unit has an **equal chance** of being selected, so personal choice does not enter.
bullets: **Lottery method:** number the units on slips, mix well, draw the required number.
**Random number table:** read off numbers from a table of random digits and pick the units with those numbers.
slides.narration: In random sampling, each unit of the population has an equal chance of being chosen, so the investigator cannot favour any unit. In the lottery method, you write every unit number on a slip, mix the slips well, and draw as many as the sample needs. With a random number table, you read numbers from the table and select the units that carry those numbers.

slides.heading: The lottery method, step by step

nodes.label: Number each unit and write it on a slip
Fold and mix the slips well
Draw slips one by one without looking
Stop at the planned sample size

visual.alt: Flow of the lottery method: number each unit on a slip, mix the slips, draw them one by one, and stop at the planned sample size
visual.caption: Lottery method in four steps

slides.narration: Here is the lottery method in four steps. First, number each unit and write the number on a slip. Second, fold the slips and mix them thoroughly. Third, draw slips one by one without looking. Fourth, stop when you have drawn as many as the sample size requires. The units on the slips you drew form the sample.

slides.heading: Non-random sampling
slides.body_md: In **non-random sampling** the units are not chosen by a chance device, so they do **not** all have an equal chance.

rows: Investigator picks units she thinks typical
She selects the shops she feels are average
The first thirty people at a bus stand
Fixed numbers from each category; interviewer chooses within them
Meet 20 women and 30 men, any willing persons

visual.alt: Table of three non-random methods: judgement sampling, convenience sampling and quota sampling, each with how units are chosen and an imagined illustration
visual.caption: Non-random methods are open to the investigator's bias.

slides.narration: In non-random sampling a chance device does not decide. In judgement sampling, the investigator picks units she believes are typical. In convenience sampling, she takes whoever is easiest to reach. In quota sampling, interviewers must meet fixed numbers from each category but choose the individuals themselves. All three can carry the own bias of the investigator into the sample.

slides.heading: Sampling error
slides.body_md: **Sampling error** is the difference between a sample estimate and the true population value. It tends to **fall as the sample grows**, and is nil in a census.

slides.narration: A sample covers only some units, so its estimate rarely equals the true value for the whole population. The gap is the sampling error. Drawing a larger random sample usually shrinks it, because the sample resembles the population more closely. In this imagined survey of fifty shops, the larger sample of twenty has a far smaller error than the sample of ten. In a census, the error is nil.

slides.heading: Worked example 2: computing a sampling error
slides.body_md: An imagined register lists the daily milk sales of all 50 shops of Kelvapur. A random number table selects 10 shops.
bullets: The sample of 10 overstates the population mean by the sampling error.
A different random sample would give a different error.

visual.alt: Table of the worked example: ten sampled values add to 1220, the sample mean is 122.00 litres, the population mean is 120.42 litres, and the sampling error is 1.58 litres
visual.caption: Imagined survey of 10 of the 50 milk shops of Kelvapur.

slides.narration: Ten shops were drawn at random. Add their daily sales to get a total, divide by ten to find the sample mean, and compare it with the population mean from the register. The difference, sample mean minus population mean, is the sampling error. A different random sample of ten shops would give a different error.

slides.heading: Non-sampling errors
slides.body_md: **Non-sampling errors** arise in collecting and processing data, not from studying only a part. Even a census can have them.

rows: Wrong recording or measurement of answers
A sale of 84 litres written as 48
A faulty plan favours some units
Only shops on the main road are chosen
A column of sales is added wrongly

visual.alt: Table of four non-sampling errors: errors in data acquisition, non-response, sampling bias and arithmetic errors, each with an imagined illustration
visual.caption: A census can suffer from these too.

slides.narration: Non-sampling errors come from how the work is done, not from sampling itself. They include errors in data acquisition, such as recording or measuring wrongly, non-response, sampling bias from a faulty selection plan, and arithmetic errors. A bigger sample does not cure them, and a census can suffer from them too. Training, checking and follow-up are the remedies.

slides.heading: Quick check: how much is sampled?
slides.body_md: A researcher draws 10 of the 50 milk shops of Kelvapur. What percentage of the population is in the sample?
slides.narration: Divide the sample size by the population size, then express the answer as a percentage of the whole population.

slides.heading: Census of India
slides.body_md: The **Census of India** is conducted **every ten years** by the Office of the Registrar General and Census Commissioner, India.
bullets: It counts the **whole population** and collects **demographic, social and economic** data such as literacy, occupation and housing.
The first **synchronous** census, with the count made at the same time across the country, was held in **1881**.
slides.narration: The Census of India is held every ten years by the Office of the Registrar General and Census Commissioner, India. It is a count of the whole population and collects demographic, social and economic data, such as literacy, occupation and housing. The first synchronous census, in which the count was made at the same time across the country, was held in eighteen eighty one.

slides.heading: The National Sample Survey Organisation
slides.body_md: The **NSSO**, set up in **1950**, conducts nationwide **sample surveys**, called **rounds**, on consumption expenditure, employment and unemployment, and other subjects.
bullets: **Dated note (as of 2024):** after a merger in 2019, the NSSO is part of the **National Statistics Office** under the Ministry of Statistics and Programme Implementation.
slides.narration: The National Sample Survey Organisation was set up in nineteen fifty. It conducts nationwide sample surveys in rounds, on subjects such as household consumption expenditure and employment and unemployment. Note the date. As of twenty twenty four, after a merger in twenty nineteen, it forms part of the National Statistics Office under the Ministry of Statistics and Programme Implementation.

sections.heading: 1. Primary and secondary data
sections.body_md:
Statistics begins with **data**, the raw facts and figures that an investigator collects. Where the data come from decides how much they cost and how far they can be trusted.

**Primary data** are gathered first-hand by the investigator for her own enquiry. **Secondary data** were gathered by someone else and are only used by the investigator, usually from published reports.

**Comparison:** primary data are original, costlier, slower and fit the purpose exactly; secondary data are second-hand, cheaper, quicker and may not fit. Before using secondary data check **who** collected them, **for what purpose**, by **what method** and **when**.

key_terms.definition_md: The raw facts, figures and observations collected for a purpose; the raw material of statistics.
Data collected first-hand by the investigator for a specific purpose.
Data collected by someone else and used by the investigator.

sections.heading: 2. Methods of collecting primary data and the questionnaire
sections.body_md:
Three methods: **personal interview** (high response, doubts cleared, but costly and the interviewer may influence replies), **mailed questionnaire** (low cost and wide coverage, but low response and no clarification) and **telephone interview** (quick, but only people with phones and calls must be short).

A **questionnaire** is a set of questions put to respondents. Keep it **short**, order questions from **general to specific**, make them **precise and clear**, and avoid leading questions, double negatives, ambiguous words and questions that embarrass. Use **closed-ended** questions (two-way or multiple choice) and **open-ended** questions where suitable.

Before the main survey, a **pilot survey** tests the questionnaire on a few respondents and estimates cost and time.

A small trial run of a survey that tests the questionnaire and estimates cost and time.

sections.heading: 3. Population, census and sample
sections.body_md:
The **population** (universe) is the complete group of units about which information is wanted. In the **census method** every unit is studied; in the **sample method** a representative part is studied and the findings are used for the whole population.

| Point | Census | Sample |
|---|---|---|
| Cost | High for large populations | Lower |
| Time | Long | Short |
| Accuracy | No sampling error | Sampling error exists |
| Suitable when | Population small, every unit needed | Population large, funds limited, or testing destroys units |

key_terms.definition_md: The complete group of units about which information is wanted.
The method of studying every unit of the population.
A representative part of the population that is actually studied.

sections.heading: 4. Random and non-random sampling
sections.body_md:
In **random sampling** every unit has an equal chance of selection. Methods: the **lottery method** (numbered slips, well mixed, drawn one by one) and **random number tables**.

In **non-random sampling** units are not chosen by chance: **judgement sampling** (the investigator picks typical units), **convenience sampling** (whoever is easiest to reach) and **quota sampling** (fixed numbers from each category, the interviewer choosing the individuals). Non-random methods can carry the investigator's bias.

Non-random selection of the units that are easiest to reach.
Non-random selection in which fixed numbers are taken from each category.

sections.heading: 5. Errors in collecting data
sections.body_md:
**Sampling error** = sample estimate − true population value. It arises because only some units are studied, and it tends to fall as a random sample grows; it is nil in a census.

Imagined worked case: the sample of 10 Kelvapur shops has a total of 1220 litres, so the sample mean is 122.00 litres; the population mean of all 50 shops is 120.42 litres; the sampling error is 122.00 − 120.42 = **1.58 litres**. A larger sample of 20 shops gives a mean of 120.45 litres and an error of 0.03 litres.

**Non-sampling errors** come from the way data are collected and processed: errors in **data acquisition** (recording or measurement), **non-response**, **sampling bias** and **arithmetic errors**. They can occur in a census too.

**Response rate** = forms returned ÷ forms sent × 100. If 45 forms are sent and 36 return, the rate is 80 per cent.

key_terms.definition_md: The difference between a sample estimate and the true value for the population.
An error arising from collecting or processing data rather than from sampling.
The failure of chosen respondents to give answers.
A systematic tilt in the sample caused by a faulty selection plan.

sections.heading: 6. Census of India and the NSSO
sections.body_md:
The **Census of India** is conducted every **ten years** by the Office of the Registrar General and Census Commissioner, India. It collects population, demographic, social and economic data such as literacy, occupation and housing. The first synchronous census was held in **1881**.

The **National Sample Survey Organisation (NSSO)**, set up in **1950**, conducts nationwide sample surveys, in rounds, on consumption expenditure, employment and unemployment and other subjects.

*Dated note (as of 2024):* after a merger in 2019 the NSSO forms part of the National Statistics Office under the Ministry of Statistics and Programme Implementation.

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** primary data. She designed the questions, collected the replies herself and will use them for her own enquiry, so they are primary data. They become secondary data only for someone else who later borrows her table.

questions.stem_md: Compared with primary data collected afresh, secondary data are usually

options.text_md: costlier and slower, but fully suited to the purpose
more original, because they are collected by the user
cheaper and quicker to obtain, but they may not suit the exact purpose
free of any need for checking

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** cheaper and quicker to obtain, but they may not suit the exact purpose. Existing data save the time and money of a field survey, but they were collected for another purpose, with other definitions and units, so suitability and reliability must be checked. The other options describe features of primary data or wrongly say that no checking is needed.

questions.stem_md: Before using a table of vendor incomes found in an old report, an investigator in Kelvapur should first ask

options.text_md: how many pages the report has
whether the table is printed in colour
who collected it, for what purpose, by what method and when
whether the vendors still sell milk at the same lane

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** who collected it, for what purpose, by what method and when. Reliability and suitability of secondary data depend on the collector, the purpose, the method and the date. Length and printing have no bearing on quality, and the present location of vendors does not tell us whether the table was gathered carefully.

questions.stem_md: A main advantage of the personal interview method of collecting primary data is that

options.text_md: the interviewer can explain a question that the respondent finds unclear
it is the cheapest method of covering a wide area
it is free of any influence of the interviewer
it needs no trained field staff

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** the interviewer can explain a question that the respondent finds unclear. Face to face, the interviewer can clarify doubts and usually gets a good response. The method is costly and slow over a wide area, the interviewer may influence answers, and trained staff are needed, so the other options are false.

questions.stem_md: Which pair correctly describes a mailed questionnaire survey?

options.text_md: High response and clarification possible, but costly
Very quick, but limited to people with telephones
Accurate for illiterate respondents because the form is read aloud
Low cost and wide coverage, but low response and no chance to clarify

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** Low cost and wide coverage, but low response and no chance to clarify. Forms sent by post or e-mail reach many people cheaply, but many are not returned, and nobody is present to explain an unclear question. The second pair describes the personal interview and the third the telephone interview; a mailed form needs the respondent to read and write.

questions.stem_md: Which of these is a limitation of a telephone interview?

options.text_md: The interviewer must travel to every respondent
It can cover only those who have telephones, and the call cannot be long
It always gets a lower response than a mailed form
It cannot be completed in a short time

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** It can cover only those who have telephones, and the call cannot be long. Only persons with a phone can be reached and respondents will not stay on a long call. Telephone interviews need no travel, are usually quick, and often get better response than mailed forms, so the other options are wrong.

questions.stem_md: Which question for the imagined Greenfield school canteen survey is a leading question that a good questionnaire should avoid?

options.text_md: Don't you agree that the new samosas are far tastier than the old ones?
How many times a week do you buy lunch from the canteen?
Which snack do you buy most often?
Is the canteen open at a convenient time for you?

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** Don't you agree that the new samosas are far tastier than the old ones? The first question pushes the respondent towards one answer by suggesting what she should think. The other three ask for a fact or an opinion without suggesting the reply.

questions.stem_md: A questionnaire for the vendors of Kelvapur asks: Do you sell curd along with milk? (Yes / No). This is

options.text_md: an open-ended question
a closed-ended question of the two-way type
a leading question
a question with a double negative

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** a closed-ended question of the two-way type. The respondent chooses from fixed answers, here two, so it is a closed-ended two-way question. An open-ended question lets the respondent reply in her own words. Nothing in the wording suggests the answer or uses a double negative.

questions.stem_md: The main purpose of a pilot survey is to

options.text_md: replace the main survey when funds are short
check the arithmetic of the final report
test the questionnaire on a few respondents and estimate the time and cost of the main survey
select the sample by lottery

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** test the questionnaire on a few respondents and estimate the time and cost of the main survey. A pilot is a small trial run before the real survey, so faults in the questions and in the plan show up early. It does not replace the main survey, it is done before any report exists, and it is not a method of selecting units.

questions.stem_md: The imagined Madhupur Tea Growers Cooperative has 25 members and wants each member's view on a proposed change in its rules. The better method is

options.text_md: a sample, because a census always costs more than the benefit
a sample, because small groups cannot be fully studied
neither, because the group is too small to survey
a census, because the population is small and every view matters

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** a census, because the population is small and every view matters. With only 25 members, studying all of them is cheap and quick, and the decision needs every member's opinion. A sample would add sampling error without saving much. Small groups can certainly be surveyed in full.

questions.stem_md: An imagined lamp company wants to find how long its bulbs burn before failing. Testing every bulb would destroy the whole stock. The company should use

options.text_md: a census, because accuracy is the only concern
secondary data only, since bulbs cannot be tested
no method, since burning life cannot be measured
a sample survey, because testing destroys the units tested

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** a sample survey, because testing destroys the units tested. When studying a unit uses it up, only a part of the population can be tested, so a sample is the sensible choice. A census would leave nothing to sell.

questions.stem_md: The register of all 50 milk shops of Kelvapur is used for a survey of shop sales. In the vocabulary of sampling, these 50 shops are

options.text_md: a sample
a variable
the population (universe)
an error

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** the population (universe). The population is the whole group of units about which information is wanted, here the 50 shops. A sample would be some of them. A variable is a characteristic such as litres sold.

questions.stem_md: In random (probability) sampling,

options.text_md: the investigator picks the units she thinks typical
every unit of the population has an equal chance of being selected
the first people met are interviewed
fixed numbers of respondents are chosen from each category by interviewers

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** every unit of the population has an equal chance of being selected. Random selection gives each unit the same chance and leaves out personal choice. The other options describe judgement, convenience and quota sampling, which are non-random.

questions.stem_md: A surveyor interviews the first thirty people who pass the bus stand of the imagined town of Neelgiri because they are easy to reach. This is

options.text_md: convenience sampling
lottery sampling
random number table sampling
quota sampling

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** convenience sampling. Choosing whoever is easiest to reach is convenience sampling. Lottery and random number tables give equal chances to all units, and quota sampling fixes numbers for categories of respondents.

questions.stem_md: Interviewers of an imagined market survey are told to meet exactly 20 women and 30 men, choosing any willing persons they find. The method is

options.text_md: simple random sampling
quota sampling
census
pilot survey

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** quota sampling. Fixed numbers for each category, filled by the interviewers' own choice, make quota sampling, a non-random method. Random sampling would leave the choice to a chance device, and a census covers everyone.

questions.stem_md: Sampling error is the

options.text_md: mistake made in adding the figures
refusal of some respondents to answer
mistake in recording an answer wrongly
difference between a sample estimate and the true population value

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** difference between a sample estimate and the true population value. Because a sample covers only some units, its estimate usually differs a little from the value for the whole population; that gap is the sampling error. Adding mistakes, refusals and recording mistakes are non-sampling errors.

questions.stem_md: If the sample drawn at random from a population is made larger, sampling error

options.text_md: tends to fall
tends to rise
is always exactly zero
is unrelated to sample size

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** tends to fall. A larger sample covers more of the population and is likely to resemble it more closely, so the error tends to fall. It becomes zero only when the whole population is studied, and it is not guaranteed in any single draw.

questions.stem_md: In a survey of Kelvapur milk shops, several shopkeepers did not answer. This is an example of

options.text_md: a sampling error arising from sample size
an error that a census cannot have
a non-sampling error arising from non-response
a computing error in averages

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** a non-sampling error arising from non-response. Non-response is a non-sampling error: it comes from what happens during data collection, not from studying only part of the population. It can occur in a census too. It is not an arithmetic mistake.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** A census of a very large population is often not practical.

**Reason (R):** A census requires every unit to be studied, which needs much time, money and staff.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** Both statements are true, and the cost in time, money and staff of studying every single unit is exactly why a census of a huge population is seldom practical.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** Random sampling keeps the investigator's personal choice out of the selection of units.

**Reason (R):** Judgement sampling lets the investigator choose the units she considers typical.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** Both statements are true. But R describes another method, a non-random one, and does not explain why chance selection removes personal choice; the explanation lies in equal chances for every unit.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** Secondary data are always more reliable than primary data.

**Reason (R):** Secondary data usually cost less and take less time to obtain than primary data.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** A is false: reliability depends on the collector, the method and the purpose, and some secondary data are weak. R is true as a general statement about cost and time.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** A mailed questionnaire can reach many respondents at a low cost.

**Reason (R):** In a mailed questionnaire the investigator can clarify every doubt of the respondent on the spot.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** A is true: forms travel cheaply to scattered respondents. R is false: nobody is present when a form is filled, so doubts cannot be cleared, which is one of the weaknesses of the method.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** Enlarging a randomly drawn sample tends to lower the sampling error.

**Reason (R):** As the sample moves closer to the whole population, its estimate tends to move closer to the population value.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** Both are true and R explains A: a bigger share of the units makes the sample more like the population, so the gap between estimate and truth tends to shrink.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** The NSSO collects its data from sample surveys, not by counting the whole country.

**Reason (R):** The NSSO conducts surveys in rounds on subjects such as household consumption expenditure and employment.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** Both are true. The subjects and the round system describe what the NSSO surveys, not why it uses samples; the reason is that a full count of every household for every subject would be too costly and slow.

questions.stem_md: True or false? A personal interview often gets a high response and lets the interviewer clear doubts, but it can be costly and the interviewer may sway the replies.

options.text_md: True
False

questions.solution_md: **True.** Both the strengths and the weaknesses stated are the standard ones for this method.

questions.stem_md: True or false? For the same large population, a census usually costs less and takes less time than a sample survey.

options.text_md: True
False

questions.solution_md: **False.** A census studies every unit, so for a large population it usually needs more money and time than a sample survey.

questions.stem_md: True or false? The Census of India is conducted by the National Sample Survey Organisation.

options.text_md: True
False

questions.solution_md: **False.** The Census of India is conducted by the Office of the Registrar General and Census Commissioner, India; the NSSO carries out sample surveys.

questions.stem_md: True or false? In simple random sampling each unit of the population has the same chance of being chosen.

options.text_md: True
False

questions.solution_md: **True.** That equal chance is the defining feature of random selection.

questions.stem_md: A small trial run of a survey, used to test the questionnaire before the main survey, is called a ___ survey.
questions.solution_md: The trial run is a pilot survey.

questions.stem_md: The complete group of units that an enquiry wants to know about is called the statistical ___.
questions.solution_md: It is the population, also called the universe.

questions.stem_md: Judgement sampling, convenience sampling and ___ sampling are the three non-random methods named in this chapter.
questions.solution_md: The third non-random method is quota sampling.

questions.stem_md: Match each imagined survey situation with the method of collecting primary data it describes.

options.text_md: Surveyors visit each stall in the Sundarwadi market and ask the questions face to face
Forms are posted to 300 farmers spread over many villages, to be returned by post
An enquirer rings 40 office workers to ask three quick questions on commuting

questions.solution_md: **Key:** (a)–(q), (b)–(r), (c)–(p). Face-to-face questions are a personal interview; forms sent out and returned are a mailed questionnaire; a quick set of questions over the phone is a telephone interview.

questions.stem_md: Match each source of secondary data with its description.

options.text_md: Census of India
National Sample Survey Organisation
Economic Survey
Labour Bureau

match_right.text_md: Reports on labour matters such as wages and employment
Count of the whole population every ten years
Yearly review of the economy brought out by the Ministry of Finance
Nationwide sample surveys carried out in rounds

questions.solution_md: **Key:** (a)–(q), (b)–(s), (c)–(r), (d)–(p). The Census counts everyone at ten-year intervals, the NSSO samples households in rounds, the Economic Survey reviews the economy each year, and the Labour Bureau reports on labour conditions.

questions.stem_md: Arrange these stages of an imagined canteen survey in a sensible order.

options.text_md: Revise the questionnaire and run the main survey
Draft the questionnaire
Try the questionnaire in a pilot survey
Decide the purpose of the survey and the population to be studied

questions.solution_md: **Correct order:** (d) → (b) → (c) → (a). The purpose and population come first; then the draft; then a small trial; and only after the faults are fixed does the main survey begin.

marking_scheme.step: Complete correct sequence (all items in place)

questions.stem_md: Arrange the steps of the lottery method for drawing a sample of shops from the register of an imagined town.

options.text_md: Stop when the required sample size has been drawn
Draw slips one at a time without looking
Fold the slips and mix them well in a box
Give every shop a number and write it on a slip of paper

questions.solution_md: **Correct order:** (d) → (c) → (b) → (a). Slips must exist before they can be mixed, mixing comes before drawing, and drawing stops at the planned sample size.

marking_scheme.step: Complete correct sequence (all items in place)

questions.stem_md: An imagined researcher draws a sample of 10 shops from the 50 milk shops of Kelvapur. What percentage of the population is covered by the sample?
questions.solution_md:
Step 1: Sample size ÷ population size = 10 ÷ 50 = 0.2.
Step 2: As a percentage, 0.2 × 100 = 20 per cent.

questions.stem_md: A researcher draws 10 of the 50 milk shops of Kelvapur with a random number table. Their daily milk sales (litres, imagined) are 140, 112, 129, 105, 126, 106, 127, 111, 140, 124. Find the mean daily sale of the sample.
questions.solution_md:
Step 1: Sum of the 10 values = 1220.
Step 2: Sample mean = 1220 ÷ 10 = 122.00 litres per day.

questions.stem_md: The register of all 50 milk shops of Kelvapur shows a population mean daily sale of 120.42 litres. A sample of 10 shops gives a sample mean of 122.00 litres. Find the sampling error, sample mean minus population mean, in litres.
questions.solution_md:
Step 1: Sampling error = sample mean − population mean.
Step 2: 122.00 − 120.42 = 1.58 litres per day. The sample overstates the true mean by this amount.

questions.stem_md: The imagined Pratap Dairy Cooperative mails a questionnaire to 45 member families and receives 36 completed forms back. Find the response rate as a percentage of the forms sent.
questions.solution_md:
Step 1: Response rate = forms returned ÷ forms sent × 100.
Step 2: 36 ÷ 45 × 100 = 80 per cent. The other 9 forms are non-response.

questions.stem_md: Define primary data and secondary data. Give one imagined example of each from a study of the milk trade of Kelvapur.
questions.solution_md: A definition and an example for each.

answer.model_answer_md: **Primary data** are collected first-hand by the investigator for her own enquiry, such as questions put to Kelvapur vendors about their daily sales. **Secondary data** were collected by someone else and are only used by the investigator, such as sales figures taken from a published dairy board report.

marking_scheme.step: Primary data defined with an example
Secondary data defined with an example

questions.stem_md: What is a pilot survey? State two things an investigator can learn from running one before surveying the vendors of Sundarwadi.
questions.solution_md: Meaning, then two uses such as testing questions and estimating time and cost.

answer.model_answer_md: A **pilot survey** is a small trial run of the enquiry on a few respondents before the main survey. It shows whether the **questions are clear** and in a sensible order, and it gives an estimate of the **time and cost** the main survey will need.

questions.stem_md: Distinguish a closed-ended question from an open-ended one, using the imagined Greenfield canteen survey for an example of each.
questions.solution_md: Fixed choices versus free reply, each with an example.

answer.model_answer_md: A **closed-ended** question offers fixed answers to choose from, for example: Do you buy lunch at the canteen? (Yes / No). An **open-ended** question lets the student reply in her own words, for example: What one change would you like in the canteen menu?

questions.stem_md: Explain what is meant by a census and by a sample, taking the 50 milk shops of Kelvapur as the population.
questions.solution_md: Census means all units; sample means a representative part.

answer.model_answer_md: In a **census** every one of the 50 shops would be studied. In a **sample** only a representative part of them, say 10 shops, is studied, and the findings are used to say something about all 50.

questions.stem_md: Describe how the lottery method could be used to select 10 shops out of 50 numbered shops in an imagined market.
questions.solution_md: Slips, mixing, drawing the required number, equal chance.

answer.model_answer_md: Write each shop number on an identical slip, fold the slips and **mix them well** in a box. Then **draw 10 slips one by one** without looking. The shops on those slips form the sample, and every shop had the same chance of being drawn.

questions.stem_md: What is quota sampling? Why is it called a non-random method?
questions.solution_md: Fixed numbers per category; non-random because the interviewer chooses.

answer.model_answer_md: In **quota sampling** the investigator is told to include fixed numbers of respondents from each category, such as 20 women and 30 men. It is non-random because the interviewer **chooses the individuals** herself, so units do not all have an equal chance of selection.

questions.stem_md: What is sampling error? How can an investigator reduce it?
questions.solution_md: Definition and the effect of a larger sample.

answer.model_answer_md: **Sampling error** is the difference between a sample estimate and the true value for the whole population, arising because only some units are studied. It can be reduced by **drawing a larger random sample**, and it disappears only in a census.

questions.stem_md: Explain non-response as a source of error in a mailed questionnaire survey. Suggest one way to lower it.
questions.solution_md: Meaning, its effect, and one remedy such as reminders.

answer.model_answer_md: **Non-response** occurs when chosen respondents do not return the form or do not answer some questions, so the replies may not represent the whole group. It can be lowered by **sending reminders** or by following up with a short call or visit.

questions.stem_md: Which office conducts the Census of India, how often is it held, and what kinds of data does it collect?
questions.solution_md: Agency, interval and kinds of data.

answer.model_answer_md: The census is conducted by the **Office of the Registrar General and Census Commissioner, India**, once in **ten years**. It collects data on the population, such as its size, age and sex, and social and economic data like literacy, occupation and housing.

questions.stem_md: What is the National Sample Survey Organisation? Name two subjects on which it has conducted surveys.
questions.solution_md: Sample survey body set up in 1950, two subjects.

answer.model_answer_md: The **NSSO**, set up in 1950, conducts nationwide **sample surveys** in rounds. Two subjects on which it has surveyed households are **consumption expenditure** and **employment and unemployment**.

questions.stem_md: Compare primary and secondary data on any three points, with reference to a study of vendors in an imagined town.
questions.solution_md: Any three points of difference, each stated for both kinds of data.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **Originality:** primary data are original, collected by the investigator; secondary data were collected earlier by someone else.
2. **Cost and time:** primary collection through field visits is costly and slow; secondary data are cheaper and quicker.
3. **Suitability:** primary data fit the enquiry exactly; secondary data may use other definitions and must be checked for reliability.

questions.stem_md: Compare the personal interview and the mailed questionnaire on cost, response and clarification of doubts.
questions.solution_md: One point each for cost, response and clarification.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **Cost:** a personal interview is costly because of travel and trained staff; a mailed questionnaire is cheap.
2. **Response:** interviews get a high response; mailed forms often get a low one.
3. **Clarification:** the interviewer can explain unclear questions on the spot; with a mailed form nobody is present to help.

questions.stem_md: State three points to be remembered while framing a questionnaire for a survey of the imagined Greenfield school canteen, with an illustration for each.
questions.solution_md: Any three well-illustrated points of good questionnaire design.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **Keep it short:** ask only what the survey needs, say eight questions rather than forty.
2. **Order from general to specific:** begin with whether the student uses the canteen, then ask about prices.
3. **Avoid leading questions:** ask Which snack do you buy most often? instead of Don't you love the samosas?

questions.stem_md: Hillview School, an imagined school, has 240 girls and 360 boys. A quota sample of 50 students is to be taken in proportion to the number of girls and boys. Find the quota for each group and explain why the method is non-random.
questions.solution_md: Girls quota 20, boys quota 30, and the reason for non-randomness.

answer.model_answer_md: Total students = 240 + 360 = 600. Girls quota = 50 × 240 ÷ 600 = **20**; boys quota = 50 × 360 ÷ 600 = **30**. It is non-random because within each quota the interviewer **picks the students herself**, so not every student has an equal chance.

questions.stem_md: Distinguish random sampling from non-random sampling on any three points. Name one method of each.
questions.solution_md: Three differences with one named method of each kind.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **Chance:** in random sampling every unit has an equal chance; in non-random sampling it does not.
2. **Who selects:** random selection is by a chance device, such as the lottery method; non-random selection rests on the investigator's own judgement or convenience.
3. **Bias:** random sampling limits personal bias; non-random sampling is open to it. Example of a non-random method: quota sampling.

marking_scheme.step: Bias, with a named method of each kind

questions.stem_md: How does the Census of India differ from the surveys of the NSSO in coverage, frequency and the kind of information collected?
questions.solution_md: One point each for coverage, frequency and information.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **Coverage:** the census counts the whole population; the NSSO surveys only a sample of households.
2. **Frequency:** the census is held once in ten years; NSSO surveys are carried out in rounds, so topics can be revisited more often.
3. **Information:** the census gathers population, demographic, social and economic data; the NSSO surveys consumption expenditure, employment and similar subjects.

questions.stem_md: Distinguish between primary and secondary data on five points, with imagined examples from a study of the milk vendors of Kelvapur.
questions.solution_md: Five points of difference, with an example for at least one kind of data.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **Meaning:** primary data are gathered first-hand for the enquiry; secondary data were gathered by others, for example from a dairy board report.
2. **Originality:** primary data are original; secondary data are second-hand.
3. **Cost:** collecting primary data from vendors is costly; secondary data are cheaper.
4. **Time:** a field survey takes long; borrowed data are quick.
5. **Suitability and reliability:** primary data fit the purpose and the investigator knows how they were collected; secondary data need checking for definitions, method and date.

questions.stem_md: Describe three methods of collecting primary data, stating one merit and one demerit of each.
questions.solution_md: Three methods, each with a merit and a demerit; marks for description and for the pairs.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **Personal interview:** questions are put face to face. Merit: high response and doubts can be cleared. Demerit: costly, and the interviewer may influence answers.
2. **Mailed questionnaire:** forms are sent out and returned. Merit: low cost and wide coverage. Demerit: low response, and no clarification is possible.
3. **Telephone interview:** respondents are asked by phone. Merit: quick. Demerit: limited to those with telephones, and the interview must be short.

marking_scheme.step: Mailed questionnaire with merit and demerit

questions.stem_md: Explain the points to be kept in mind while preparing a questionnaire. Show how they apply to an imagined questionnaire of the Greenfield school canteen.
questions.solution_md: Five good practices of questionnaire design, each tied to the canteen illustration.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **Short:** keep only the questions the canteen survey needs.
2. **Order:** move from general to specific, for example from how often a student buys lunch to opinions on prices.
3. **Precise and clear:** ask how many days a week, not whether she often buys.
4. **Avoid leading, double-negative, ambiguous or embarrassing questions.**
5. **Mix question types:** closed-ended for easy tabulation and open-ended where free comments help.

questions.stem_md: "A census always gives better results than a sample survey, so a sample should never be preferred." Evaluate this statement.
questions.solution_md: Merit of a census, its limits, a case where only a sample is possible, and a reasoned judgement.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. A census has **no sampling error**, so for a small population such as a cooperative of 25 members it is the better choice.
2. For a large population it needs far more **time, money and staff**.
3. A hurried census can have **more non-sampling errors**, such as careless recording.
4. If studying a unit destroys it, as with testing bulbs, a **sample is the only choice**.
5. The statement is **too strong**: the choice depends on population size, cost, time, accuracy needed and whether units are destroyed.

marking_scheme.step: Cost and time of a census for large populations
Non-sampling errors can rise in a very large census
A case where a sample is unavoidable

questions.stem_md: Explain sampling error and the main non-sampling errors. How does enlarging a random sample affect each kind?
questions.solution_md: Definition of each kind, the four non-sampling errors, and the different effect of sample size.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **Sampling error** is the gap between what a sample shows and the true figure for the population. A larger random sample tends to **reduce** it.
2. **Non-sampling errors** arise in collecting and processing data, namely errors in **data acquisition** such as wrong recording or measurement, **non-response**, **sampling bias** from a faulty selection plan, and **arithmetic errors**.
3. A larger sample does **not cure** these, and a bigger field operation may even add more of them. Careful training, checking and follow-up are the remedies.

options.text_md: Reserve Bank of India
National Sample Survey Organisation
Office of the Registrar General and Census Commissioner, India
Labour Bureau

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** Office of the Registrar General and Census Commissioner, India. The census is run by the Office of the Registrar General and Census Commissioner. The central bank deals with money and banking, the NSSO conducts sample surveys, and the Labour Bureau reports on labour matters.

questions.stem_md: The first synchronous census of India was held in the year
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** 1881. The count of the first synchronous census was made across the country at one time, in 1881. The year 1950 is when the NSSO was set up; the other years are not linked to the first synchronous census.

questions.stem_md: The National Sample Survey Organisation was set up in
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** 1950. The NSSO was set up in 1950. The year 1881 belongs to the first synchronous census, 1935 to the founding of the central bank, and 2019 is the year the NSSO was merged into the National Statistics Office.

questions.stem_md: The NSSO is best known for conducting

options.text_md: a full count of every household once in ten years
nationwide sample surveys, called rounds, on consumption expenditure and employment
yearly reviews of the economy for Parliament
the issue of currency notes

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** nationwide sample surveys, called rounds, on consumption expenditure and employment. The NSSO works through sample surveys in rounds. A full ten-year count is the work of the census office, the yearly review is the Economic Survey, and currency is issued by the central bank.

questions.stem_md: As of 2024, the NSSO is part of the

options.text_md: National Statistics Office under the Ministry of Statistics and Programme Implementation
Office of the Registrar General and Census Commissioner
Reserve Bank of India
Labour Bureau

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** National Statistics Office under the Ministry of Statistics and Programme Implementation. Following a merger in 2019, the NSSO functions within the National Statistics Office under the Ministry of Statistics and Programme Implementation. It is not part of the census office, the central bank or the Labour Bureau.

Both are held once in ten years

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** The census covers the whole population, while NSSO surveys study a sample. The census is a complete count held every ten years, while NSSO surveys are sample surveys conducted in rounds. The other statements swap or blur these features.
